name: Retractive headgear avoidance

lead: Retractive headgear avoidance is the position, associated with orthotropics, that appliances which pull the upper jaw back, together with removing teeth to make room, can leave the face flatter or more recessed. People who follow it seek orthodontic care that expands the arches and aims to preserve forward growth, in the hope of a more projected midface and jawline.

The idea was developed by British orthodontist John Mew and carried into online culture by his son Mike Mew and the mewing trend. Mainstream orthodontists generally attribute crowding mainly to genetics and report that the evidence for orthotropic treatment is inadequate.

paras: In practice this means that parents and teens choose practitioners who use palatal expansion, posture-focused appliances and diet and tongue-posture advice rather than extractions with retractive headgear, and ask about a clinic's approach before treatment begins. Adults who read about it online often use it to interpret their own past treatment.

Orthodontic professional bodies do not support orthotropic claims, and a delayed or different treatment plan can change outcomes for crowding or bite problems. Anyone weighing treatment options can discuss them with a licensed orthodontist.

chain: Aim to keep upper jaw growing forward
angle.text: Followers choose expansion-based, posture-focused treatment in the belief that it preserves a forward-set midface and a more defined jawline. The payoff is a facial profile they describe as more projected than extraction-and-headgear outcomes.

lead: Retractive headgear avoidance is a stance within orthotropics that holds that appliances which restrain or pull back the upper jaw, and extraction of teeth to relieve crowding, can harm facial growth. Those who hold it prefer treatment that widens the arches and encourages forward growth, hoping to keep the midface and jaw well projected.[1]

The view traces to John Mew (1928-2025), the British orthodontist who founded orthotropics. According to Wikipedia, he argued that standard mechanics straightened teeth without addressing the cause of crowding and sometimes damaged the face, naming extractions, fixed appliances with elastics and retractive headgear.[1] His son Mike Mew helped spread the ideas through the mewing trend after 2019.[1]

Mainstream orthodontists have opposed these views, generally attributing crooked teeth mainly to genetics, and report that evidence for orthotropic treatment is inadequate.[1] Headgear itself has uses in orthodontics, such as reverse-pull facemasks that move the upper jaw forward, which the wiki covers separately.

paras: Retractive headgear is an orthodontic appliance worn with straps that applies backward force on the upper jaw or teeth. Avoidance advocates see it as moving the face in the opposite direction from the forward growth they want, and they extend the same concern to extractions and to fixed appliances used with elastics.[1]
Orthotropic practitioners instead describe palatal expanders, dietary changes and a resting tongue posture as ways to widen and advance the upper jaw.[1]

John Mew developed orthotropics from the 1960s onward, arguing that malocclusion is a postural, environmental condition rather than mainly genetic.[1] He faced disciplinary and legal disputes with British dental authorities across his career, including a 1987 High Court appeal he won and a 2010 General Dental Council reprimand for advertising.[1]
Mike Mew popularised mewing, a do-it-yourself tongue-posture practice, in 2019 through social media, and the no-extraction, no-headgear stance travelled alongside it in looksmaxxing forums.[1]

Proponents say retractive headgear and premolar extractions can leave patients with a recessed midface, narrower arches and a weaker jawline in later life. They often cite individual before-and-after photographs.[1]

The orthodontic mainstream, including British orthodontists who opposed Mew, attributes crowding mainly to genetics and holds that evidence for orthotropic treatment is inadequate.[1] The Wikipedia article notes that parts of the theory are considered plausible but not established as an alternative to established treatments.[1]
No studies found. Trials of headgear and facemask therapy exist in mainstream orthodontics, but none test the avoidance stance as a facial-growth strategy.

lore.intro: In forums the stance appears as advice to avoid extractions and headgear and to seek expansion-based care, often tied to orthotropic clinics.[1]

claims.claim: Extractions plus retractive headgear flatten the face

timeline.event: John Mew wins a High Court appeal against an NHS finding of inappropriate treatment.[1]
The General Dental Council reprimands John Mew over advertisements.[1]
Mewing gains social-media attention, spreading orthotropic ideas.[1]
